entries.title: West Virginia’s members of Congress refuse to say whether they’ll work with Democrats on reversing Medicaid cuts
entries.summary:
West Virginia is one of the states hit hardest by Medicaid cuts. Its Congressional delegation wouldn’t say if they’d work to reverse them.

West Virginia’s members of Congress refuse to say whether they’ll work with Democrats on reversing Medicaid cuts  appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
Members of Congress who represent West Virginia refuse to publicly comment on whether they’ll work with Democrats on reversing Medicaid cuts.

With a new majority in Congress, Democratic leaders say they plan to help people afford healthcare by undoing massive Medicaid cuts that were part of the spending law, known as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” that passed under Republican control last year. 

An estimated 40,000 to 75,000 Medicaid-covered West Virginians will lose health insurance by 2028, due to new work requirements and more frequent renewals. 

All members of West Virginia’s Congressional delegation — Sen. Jim Justice, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, Congressperson Riley Moore and Congressperson Carol Miller — voted in favor of the spending law. Almost one-third of their constituents rely on Medicaid. 

None of them responded to multiple requests to answer questions about working with Democrats and their positions on repealing the cuts. 

Prior to passage of the law, Republicans said the Medicaid changes were meant to get rid of fraud, waste and abuse.

Moore said the bill protected Medicaid and only people who didn’t want to work would lose coverage. Justice made similar comments.

In explaining her support, Capito said she’d talked with hospitals and wanted to get rid of fraud and add the work requirement.

Miller praised the law for its tax cuts and frequently pens op-eds about her support for rural hospitals.

But because of the law all of them supported, many rural hospitals are now having to downsize.

And only 2.5% of the nearly $1 trillion the bill cuts from Medicaid was aimed at fraud, waste and abuse — most often committed by healthcare providers, not patients. Most adults on Medicaid are working.

The Urban Institute and Robert Wood Johnson Foundation note that coverage losses will make it harder for people to get healthcare, including preventive care and treatment for chronic conditions, making it more difficult to work.

The law is also expected to cut jobs and close hospitals, filling emergency rooms and free clinics.

Earlier this week, Capito posted on X about the “Big Beautiful Bill” and one part of it related to healthcare, the Rural Health Transformation Program fund.

Tuesday, when health officials announced West Virginia’s year two rural health fund award of $202 million, she said she was pleased to see the announcement, which she said wouldn’t be possible without the law.

Members of Congress tacked on that $50 billion fund to the bill after intense lobbying by hospitals. And while Capito had said that fund and help for hospitals was part of the reason she supported it, only a small fraction of the fund benefits hospitals, and hospitals now say they are having to cut services because of the law.

That $50 billion is also temporary, while the Medicaid cuts, unless reversed by Congress, are permanent. 

The spending bill passed by West Virginia’s Congressional delegation cuts nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid across the country over ten years, including an estimated $6.5 billion in West Virginia. West Virginia’s hospitals alone are expected to lose $1 billion a year.

West Virginia’s members of Congress refuse to say whether they’ll work with Democrats on reversing Medicaid cuts  appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.

entries.title: West Virginia says it will stop taking survivors’ benefits from foster kids
entries.summary:
Patrick Morrisey announced that West Virginia will stop taking foster care survivors’ Social Security benefits

West Virginia says it will stop taking survivors’ benefits from foster kids appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey says starting January 1, the state will stop intercepting federal survivors’ benefits from foster kids and instead preserve them, so the kids will have them to use when they exit care. 

Earlier this year, as part of an ongoing investigation into the state’s troubled foster care system, Mountain State Spotlight reported that the state is one of a shrinking number that still takes the benefits, money their deceased parents earned and paid into the federal Social Security system. The state’s foster care policy considers it a resource that can be put toward the cost of care. Applying for these benefits is one of many tasks that falls to a child’s caseworker. But many kids aren’t even aware the money is being paid on their behalf. 

In announcing the news, the governor said approximately 42 kids currently in care receive these benefits, amounting to about $402,700 annually. That’s a small percentage of what the state spends on the foster care system, but having that money set aside could make a big difference for an individual child transitioning out of foster care. 

“For a young person preparing to leave foster care, that money can make a meaningful difference,” Morrisey said in his announcement Thursday. “It can help provide a financial foundation as they move into adulthood, whether they’re continuing their education, finding a job or just living an independent life.”

Current foster care policy requires any benefit money that’s left over to be set aside in an account, but Mountain State Spotlight spoke with a former CPS worker who said she rarely saw any money left. The story also detailed the opportunities the money can provide: one former foster kid was able to get access to her saved survivors’ benefits with the help of a dedicated guardian ad litem. She bought a used car and credits the money with helping set her on a successful path.

“These kids have gotten the short end of the stick,” attorney Cathy Wallace told Mountain State Spotlight in June. “They’ve lost their family a lot of times, or they’ve lost a good chunk of their childhood. That money can make the difference in helping them get to school, buy books. It could get them transportation, so they could actually have a job. It gives them just a tiny leg up.”

It’s a leg up that many former foster kids need. A 2025 Mountain State Spotlight investigation found the state had returned millions of federal dollars that were meant to help kids exit the system and build successful adult lives. 

The movement to stop taking Social Security benefits has gotten bipartisan support. Some state legislatures have acted, while in other states, governors have issued executive orders. Nearly a year ago, Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams sent Morrisey a letter urging him to take action. Adams lauded Thursday’s announcement, and urged the remaining 10 states that still intercept foster kids’ benefits to take action. 

West Virginia says it will stop taking survivors’ benefits from foster kids appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.

entries.title: Hundreds of mines stopped producing coal decades ago. They still haven’t been cleaned up.
entries.summary:
A new federal government report confirms concerns that coal companies are not restoring mine sites for long periods, though production is completed.

Hundreds of mines stopped producing coal decades ago. They still haven’t been cleaned up. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
Hundreds of mines across Appalachia haven’t produced a single ton of coal for a quarter-century, but haven’t been cleaned up as required by law, a new federal audit found.

Coal operators haven’t fully reclaimed thousands of acres of these mines. Federal and state regulators haven’t forced action or proposed any systemic effort to remedy the problem, according to the long-awaited audit by the U.S. Government Accountability Office.

GAO investigators warned that impacts and reclamation liabilities of these mine sites are unclear because the federal agency charged with enforcing strip mining rules “does not systemically track or document this information.”

In a 57-page report, the GAO harshly criticized the Interior Department’s Office of Surface Mining, Reclamation and Enforcement for a variety of problems, from not setting clear standards for the timing of mine cleanups to stopping publication in 2020 of a legally required annual report about progress toward meeting mandated environmental standards for the coal industry.

“OSMRE does not fully assess or communicate progress toward meeting its reclamation goals,” the GAO report said. “OSMRE does not have a complete picture of the status of reclamation nationwide.”

Interior and OSMRE officials did not respond to questions about the GAO report. 

The GAO findings echo growing concerns of coalfield citizens groups and national environmental organizations. They have been sounding alarms that mines across the country are not being cleaned up, and that operators are taking advantage of lax regulation and bankruptcy system loopholes to stick taxpayers with ballooning cleanup costs.

From the early days of coal mining, companies took what they could from the hills and hollows and moved on to the next mine, often leaving a mess for residents to live with.

In 1977, when President Jimmy Carter signed the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, that was supposed to change. The law required coal companies to clean up after themselves and restore mountains and creeks, a process known as reclamation.

But, as the GAO report outlines, as the nation relies less on coal, operators of nonproducing mines have been delaying reclamation. “Unreclaimed mining sites create risks of environmental, health, and safety hazards, and delay returning lands to other productive uses,” the report said.

The report noted that OSMRE’s staff decreased from 408 to 265 over the last two years, a reduction of 35%. 

Multiple members of Congress asked for the GAO investigation three years ago. Democratic members of the House Natural Resources Committee issued a statement saying, “Without adequate measures of reclamation liabilities or regular reporting, Congress lacks the information it needs to judge whether federal oversight is working and whether reforms are needed.”

Hundreds of mines stopped producing coal decades ago. They still haven’t been cleaned up. appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.

entries.title: Judge admonished for speaking to media about CPS understaffing: ‘Sometimes you just have to take a punch for the kids’
entries.summary:
Judge Tim Sweeney ordered health officials to his courtroom over CPS staffing and called the news. The Supreme Court has issued a warning.

Judge admonished for speaking to media about CPS understaffing: ‘Sometimes you just have to take a punch for the kids’ appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
Ritchie County Judge Tim Sweeney ordered leaders at the West Virginia Department of Human Services to his courtroom last February to compel them to address a severe shortage of child protective services workers. He then contacted the media.

Thursday, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia admonished him. 

“While Judge Sweeney’s conduct happened to concern a matter that elicits universal agreement—the well-being of children—judges who stray so far outside their role such as to violate the Code are not immunized from discipline based on the popularity or success of their misconduct,” justices wrote in an opinion delivered by Chief Justice Haley Bunn, who was referencing the Judicial Code of Conduct.

In October of 2025, Sweeney, whose district includes Pleasants, Doddridge, Ritchie and Wirt counties, ordered CPS workers to send a severely traumatized child to an out-of-state mental health treatment facility. 

The following February, when the child still hadn’t been sent, they told him the child had fallen through the cracks due to understaffing. One of them told him they had about 100 cases. 

Sweeney ordered DoHS officials to report to his courthouse to start working as case workers. He admitted he wanted those leaders to solve the understaffing problem rather than to actually take new positions.

“I think somebody needs to stand up for the public, particularly the most vulnerable members of our community — the children,” he told the Parkersburg News and Sentinel. “From a legal point of view, abuse and neglect cases are of the highest priority, and they should be, in my opinion, for the department and the government in Charleston as well.”

Sweeney’s actions came before the Supreme Court last month because they had caught the attention of the Judicial Investigation Commission, which found he violated ethics rules about speaking publicly about pending cases and warned him not to make similar comments in the future. The commission also found his Facebook activity violated the rules of judicial conduct because his posts suggested he favored police and prosecutors over defendants. 

He appealed to the Judicial Hearing Board, which also found violations.

The same month Sweeney ordered health officials to his courtroom, Kanawha County Judge Maryclaire Akers ordered former DoHS Cabinet Secretary Alex Mayer to her courtroom after hearing children had been placed in hotels and 4-H camps. Akers discussed the foster care system and the placements on MetroNews the following month.

That case also went to the Supreme Court, but was dismissed over insufficient evidence.

In Thursday’s opinion, justices found Sweeney violated the code by making statements about pending matters, undermining public confidence in the judiciary and failing to fairly uphold the law. Friday, Sweeney said he respectfully disagreed with the opinion but intended to comply.

Noting that he’s never been disciplined before, and that his intentions were noble, the court ordered Sweeney to pay for the court proceedings when issuing the admonishment. Public admonishments are a milder form of discipline for judicial misconduct, compared to others like suspension or forced retirement.

“He was cooperative and forthright in this matter, and his misconduct was neither self-promoting nor dishonest,” Bunn wrote. “And while his motivations do not justify his actions, we find that an admonishment adequately deters similar misconduct in the future and is a proportionate sanction for Judge Sweeney’s conduct viewed in its totality.”

Shortly after Sweeney ordered DoHS officials to his courtroom in February, Mayer met with him to develop a plan to resolve the staffing problem, and the hearing was canceled.

The justices noted that judges aren’t supposed to affect the outcomes of cases before them. They wrote that he had created a case by ordering health officials to his court. And then, he affected the outcome when Mayer met with him to discuss staffing.

“Sometimes you just have to take a punch for the kids,” Sweeney said Friday. “Abused and neglected children were helped and shortcomings were addressed. That was and continues to be my goal.”

Judge admonished for speaking to media about CPS understaffing: ‘Sometimes you just have to take a punch for the kids’ appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
